newsitem.title: RUSSIA: U.S., Russian novices to partner veteran on Mir.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Russian novices to partner veteran on Mir.

text.p: U.S. Navy commander Wendy Lawrence is looking forward to the mission of a lifetime on space station Mir. But it will only come off if her two Russian partners, one veteran and one novice, can fix the stricken ship first.
The three, in training at Star City outside Moscow for what promises to be the toughest assignment in the 11-year history of the station, presented an upbeat front to reporters on Wednesday.
But if the Russians fail to restore the power lost in a collision last month, it could be Mir's last mission.

Taking over as commander will be Anatoly Solovyov, 49, who has spent a remarkable 456 days in space on four Mir missions between 1988 and 1995. His predecessor, now aboard Mir, developed heart problems because of the stress.
"Maybe it's like riding a bike -- once you go once, you can ride forever," said Solovyov, who holds the title of Hero of the Soviet Union, the country's highest military honour.
His thorough knowledge of the world's only space station will be vital in repairing Mir, which lost up to half its power after colliding with one of its supply ships on June 25.

Soon after their arrival on August 7, the two Russian cosmonauts will try to reattach cables leading to solar panels on the damaged Spektr module. In September they will start planning for repairs on its punctured exterior.

A former air force pilot, Solovyov has long experience with foreign cosmonauts. He served as commander with a Bulgarian in 1988, had a Frenchman aboard in 1992, and in 1995 travelled to Mir aboard the U.S. space shuttle.
This time he is due to welcome Navy aviator Lawrence, 38, a veteran of a 1995 shuttle mission and hundreds of Navy helicopter flights. She has never been on Mir.
"Of course, I very much want to fly in space," she said, wearing a green shirt, her dark hair cut short.
"I've prepared for over a year and am very much looking forward to seeing Mir," she told reporters in fluent, though accented, Russian.
But the loss of power has put her voyage in some doubt, as U.S. officials await the outcome of the Russians' efforts to restore the electricity supply.

President Bill Clinton's top science adviser, Jack Gibbons, said last week the final decision on whether she will actually join Mir could be taken as late as a day before her scheduled September 17 launch aboard the shuttle.
The flight engineer who will lead the repair efforts -- and take many of the biggest risks -- is a newcomer to space flight, Pavel Vinogradov. At 43, he is an experienced aviation engineer.

"I love aviation, the history of aviation, astrophysics, and I love to travel, both on Earth and in space," he said in a brief interview, dressed in a double-breasted jacket and sporting a thin moustache.

Vinogradov will be the one who opens the hatch to the airless, darkened Spektr module to begin repairs on August 20, and experts say he could face dangerous chemicals or scraps floating around since the June accident. Any puncture in his space suit would mean a swift death.
"I don't think there's anything terrible inside," Vinogradov said simply. "There will be no surprises."
